title: Outage scrutiny and NHS data sovereignty
headline: Parliament is scrutinising the 13 November Microsoft outage: a Shadow Cabinet Office Minister has asked whether No 10's email and Microsoft applications were disrupted, and the Government has confirmed that NHS incident arrangements were activated and that supplier concentration is being kept under review.
summary: The Microsoft 365 disruption of 13 November is now on the parliamentary record in both Houses. Lords at the Health Bill committee stage pressed for NHS data to be treated as a “sovereign” asset, citing US-owned cloud providers and the US CLOUD Act, and a Lords answer confirmed that the encryption keys for the NHS Federated Data Platform are held in AWS infrastructure. Ministers also confirmed a new “UK Supplier” definition by January 2027 and departmental insourcing strategies to be published in April, while Sarah Green (Liberal Democrat) has asked about the draft data-centre National Policy Statement and a Buckinghamshire NSIP designation.

very_important.title: Microsoft outage: were No 10's email and associated Microsoft applications disrupted?
very_important.who: Mike Wood (Conservative, Kingswinford and South Staffordshire), Shadow Cabinet Office Minister
very_important.where: House of Commons, written question 46527 to the Cabinet Office
very_important.body: Mike Wood asks whether (a) No 10's outgoing and incoming email system and (b) associated Microsoft applications were disrupted by the Microsoft outage on Friday 13 November 2026. The question is unanswered in the evidence. The same outage features in the Lords answer on NHS reliance on Microsoft (HL5499, below), so the incident is being raised in both Houses.
very_important.why: The question names Microsoft and concerns the resilience of email and associated applications at 10 Downing Street.

very_important.title: NHS reliance on Microsoft: Government keeps “supplier concentration” under review
very_important.who: Lord Taylor of Warwick (Non-affiliated); answered by Baroness Merron (Labour), DHSC Minister
very_important.where: House of Lords, written question HL5499 “NHS: Microsoft”
very_important.body: Lord Taylor asked what steps are being taken to reduce the risks of the NHS's reliance on Microsoft systems. Baroness Merron replied that the NHS uses Microsoft alongside other suppliers. She said reliance on any major provider creates potential operational, cyber and supply-chain risks, managed through resilience, business continuity, cyber security, supplier management and incident response. She confirmed that the 24/7 incident arrangements were activated during the “global Microsoft 365 service disruption on 13 November”, and that NHS organisations used their business-continuity measures. She described NHS England's process following significant supplier incidents: working with suppliers to understand the root cause, assess lessons and identify further resilience measures. Government and NHS England will keep “supplier concentration, service resilience, and appropriate contingency arrangements under review”.
very_important.why: The answer addresses NHS supplier-concentration risk and records the activation of incident arrangements during the Microsoft disruption. It was answered on the same day as the Health Bill debate on NHS data sovereignty.

very_important.title: Health Bill: peers push for NHS data as a “sovereign data asset”, citing US-owned cloud and the CLOUD Act
very_important.who: Baroness Kidron (Crossbench); Lord Clement-Jones (Liberal Democrat); Lord Tarassenko (Crossbench); Lord Patel (Crossbench); Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (Crossbench); Lord Markham (Conservative); Earl Howe (Conservative); Baroness Merron (Labour), DHSC Minister
very_important.where: House of Lords Chamber, Health Bill committee stage (Amendments 142, 143, 172, 172C and related)
very_important.why: The debate addresses proposed controls over NHS data, supplier ownership, overseas access and encryption keys. Lord Markham supported sovereignty over data but warned against requiring UK-supplied technology.
very_important.linkText: Hansard: Health Bill, Lords committee stage, Lord Clement-Jones

very_important.title: NHS Federated Data Platform: encryption keys held in AWS infrastructure; Palantir enrolment administration roles approved
very_important.who: Lord Scriven (Liberal Democrat); answered by Baroness Merron (Labour), DHSC Minister
very_important.where: House of Lords, written questions HL5327 and HL5328
very_important.body: The Government says NHS England owns the encryption keys for the Federated Data Platform. The keys are managed through Privacy Enhancing Technology software and are “held securely within the Amazon Web Services' infrastructure”. Palantir staff cannot independently decrypt data. Five non-NHS enrolment administration role requests for access to data in the National Data Integration Tenant have been approved, all for Palantir UK staff; three such roles are currently active.
very_important.why: The answer distinguishes NHS England's ownership of the keys from their hosting within AWS infrastructure and specifies supplier-access controls. It provides context for the Health Bill debate on NHS data sovereignty.

very_important.title: Government supplier exit: new Insourcing Unit, five-year departmental insourcing strategies, and Capita and ERP dependency
very_important.who: Siân Berry (Green, Brighton Pavilion), Green Chief Whip
very_important.where: House of Commons, written questions 45030, 45031, 45032 (Cabinet Office) and 45039 (MHCLG)
very_important.body:
45030 (Civil Service Pension Scheme and Capita): Cabinet Office officials now have access to Capita's systems, the scheme is described as a “prime candidate for future insourcing”, and a Delivery Model Assessment is under way.
45031 and 45032: departments will publish five-year Insourcing Strategies in April. These will be scrutinised by a new Insourcing Unit, which will act as a centre of expertise on exiting contracts.
45039 (local authorities' dependency on Oracle and SAP ERP systems): the Government says this is a matter for councils, and the Cabinet Office is assessing guidance on insourcing.
very_important.why: The answers describe a cross-government centre of expertise on bringing services in-house and respond to questions about exit planning for digital, data and technology contracts and local-authority ERP dependency.

very_important.title: Procurement: new “UK Supplier” definition based on genuine UK presence due by January 2027
very_important.who: Martin Wrigley (Liberal Democrat, Newton Abbot), Science and Technology Committee; answered by Mark Ferguson
very_important.where: House of Commons, written questions 40446, 40449, 40451, 40493 and 44580
very_important.body: The Government accepts that the current definition of a UK supplier “is easily met by suppliers without genuine presence in the UK”. A new “UK Supplier” definition based on genuine UK economic presence will be published by January 2027. The exact criteria are still being developed, and legislation will follow when Parliamentary time allows. Question 40493 asks how a “British AI company” is defined, with reference to Budget paragraph 4.119. Question 44580 draws out that the Procurement of Innovation Playbook proposes that suppliers keep foreground intellectual property.
very_important.why: The definition remains under development and is intended to improve procurement data and supply-chain transparency. The answer says the reforms must comply with trade agreements.

very_important.title: Digital sovereignty: Government acknowledges “dominance of a few global technology firms” as a chronic risk
very_important.who: Clive Lewis (Labour, Norwich South); answered by Ian Murray (DCMS)
very_important.where: House of Commons, written questions 44193 and 44194
very_important.body: 44193: the question refers to the National Chronic Risk Register. The answer describes technological risks identified in the Chronic Risk analysis, highlighting developments resulting in “the dominance of a few global technology firms”, and points to the Sovereign AI fund, the AI hardware plan and the quantum plan as responses. 44194: the Government CTO attended Beyond GovTech in Copenhagen in November 2026, including a UK–Denmark roundtable on digital sovereignty. This builds on a memorandum of understanding signed in January 2026 between GDS and the Danish Agency for Digital Government.
very_important.why: The answers connect technology concentration with domestic sovereign capability and report UK–Danish cooperation on digital resilience.

very_important.title: EU Cloud and AI Development Act: UK seeking recognition as a trusted partner and fair access to EU cloud markets
very_important.who: Lord Taylor of Warwick (Non-affiliated); answered by Baroness Lloyd of Effra (Labour), Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
very_important.where: House of Lords, written question HL5329
very_important.body: The Government says it is engaging with the EU on its Technology Sovereignty Package. Current efforts focus on making sure the proposed EU Cloud and AI Development Act recognises trusted third-country partners and protects fair UK access to EU cloud markets.
very_important.why: The answer concerns a proposed EU measure and the Government's stated objective of fair access for UK businesses. Today's Lords debate is on the 20 November EU–UK summit.

very_important.title: Data centres: questions on the draft National Policy Statement and the Wapseys Wood NSIP designation
very_important.who: Sarah Green (Liberal Democrat, Chesham and Amersham), Public Accounts Committee
very_important.where: House of Commons, written questions 46685, 46687 (data-centre NPS), 46665 (DESNZ), 46686 (Defra) and 46664 (MHCLG)
very_important.body:
46685: what is the maximum period for which on-site gas generation counts as “temporary” under paragraph 159 of the draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, and would up to 15 years before grid connection qualify?
46687: whether the minister plans to set limits on continuous low-frequency noise from data centres and their on-site gas generation near homes in the draft NPS.
46665: what assessment has been made of the compatibility of on-site fossil-fuel generation with climate targets?
46686: what assessment the Environment Agency has made of the impact of deep piling through former landfill sites for data centres in seriously water-stressed areas on groundwater and chalk streams.
46664: what economic and infrastructure impact assessment MHCLG made of the proposed SDC M40 Campus at Wapseys Wood, Buckinghamshire, when determining its Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project designation.
very_important.why: The questions cover proposed noise limits, on-site energy generation, groundwater risks and the economic and infrastructure assessment for the Wapseys Wood designation.

debates.title: Code of practice on public authorities sharing data with digital verification services
debates.who: Baroness Lloyd of Effra (Labour), Minister at the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade; Lord Clement-Jones (Liberal Democrat); Lord Markham (Conservative); Viscount Stansgate (Labour)
debates.body: The draft code under Section 49 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 governs the “information gateway” under Section 45. Through it, public authorities such as the Passport Office, DVLA and General Register Office can share identity data with registered, certified digital verification services (DVS). Lord Clement-Jones did not oppose the code. He said the national digital ID scheme had been abandoned in July. He described the gateway as, in practice, the main route for proving identity online and pressed for stronger oversight. Lord Markham supported the code but asked that verification give yes/no answers rather than disclose underlying data, and raised cyber risk. The minister said digital identities remain optional, DVS must be independently certified against the trust framework, and the Office for Digital Identities and Attributes has worked closely with the NCSC.
debates.why: The code concerns public-authority identity-data sharing with registered DVS and certification and security requirements for those services.
debates.linkText: Hansard: DVS code of practice, Lord Clement-Jones

debates.who: Lord Leong (Labour), Minister at the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade; Lord Clement-Jones (Liberal Democrat); Lord Hunt of Wirral (Conservative)
debates.why: The minister explicitly ruled out an enforcement grace period and warned that early conduct may be considered in enforcement action.

debates.title: EDITH AI breast-screening trial
debates.who: Baroness Nargund (Labour); Lord Tarassenko (Crossbench); Baroness Blackwood of North Oxford (Conservative); Baroness Merron (Labour), DHSC Minister
debates.where: House of Lords Chamber, oral question
debates.body: The minister described EDITH as the world's largest trial of whether AI can safely help NHS experts detect breast cancer earlier, always working with human readers. Lord Tarassenko asked for the full protocol to be published. Baroness Blackwood, who declared that she chairs Genomics England and HDRS, asked about post-market surveillance of AI diagnostics. Baroness Nargund raised representativeness and bias. The minister cited acceptance of all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare.
debates.why: The trial was also cited by Baroness Kidron in the Health Bill debate about NHS data and US-owned suppliers.

debates.title: PMQs: Prime Minister cites the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill on national resilience
debates.where: House of Commons Chamber, Prime Minister's Questions (Engagements)
debates.body: Responding on resilience, the Prime Minister pointed to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, which is going through the House, to protect critical infrastructure. The Prime Minister also mentioned the Be Ready campaign and said the Liaison Committee would be addressed on resilience on Monday.
debates.why: The intervention links the Bill, the Be Ready campaign and the planned Liaison Committee appearance to national resilience.
debates.linkText: Hansard: PMQs, Prime Minister on resilience

questions.title: HMRC data centre exit, and AI-led performance checks in the Senior Civil Service
questions.who: Mike Wood (Conservative, Kingswinford and South Staffordshire), Shadow Cabinet Office Minister
questions.where: House of Commons, written questions 39256 and 44503
questions.body: 39256: Efficio Ltd was paid to support joint work between the Cabinet Office Complex Transactions Team and HMRC on the “Data Centre Exit programme”. Its work was to review historic software, licensing and contracts to support migration from legacy infrastructure. 44503: Responses to the AI-led Senior Civil Service performance dip-testing commission are being reviewed; results are expected in December 2026.
questions.why: The answer describes work reviewing software, licences and contracts to support migration from legacy infrastructure.

questions.title: DeepSeek and the US notice of order
questions.who: Viscount Camrose (Conservative), Shadow Cabinet Office Minister for AI and Cyber
questions.where: House of Lords, written question HL5233
questions.body: Viscount Camrose asked about DeepSeek in light of US notice of order 2026-21447 of 20 October. The Government replied that it does not comment on the detail of confidential discussions with international partners.
questions.why: This records a question about security discussions concerning DeepSeek; the answer does not disclose the detail of those discussions.

questions.title: Further AI questions: labour market, political content moderation and AI literacy in schools
questions.where: House of Lords, written questions HL5276, HL5857 and HL5855
questions.date: HL5276 tabled 2026-11-11 and answered; HL5857 and HL5855 tabled 2026-11-25
questions.body: HL5276 asks about housing-market volatility caused by AI-related labour-market shocks; the Government pointed to the AI Economics Institute. Lord Taylor has also tabled questions on AI moderation of political content (HL5857) and AI literacy in secondary schools (HL5855).
questions.why: The questions address AI's economic effects, political content moderation and school AI literacy.
questions.linkText: Written question HL5276 (see also HL5855, HL5857)

questions.title: Cyber threats to critical national infrastructure
questions.body: The answer says Dan Jarvis chaired a closed-door threat briefing with chief executives of critical national infrastructure (CNI) operators. It also notes that the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill was introduced on 12 November 2025.
questions.why: This is engagement on CNI cyber resilience linked to the CS&R Bill.

questions.title: £70m for the National Exposure and Real Time Vulnerability (NERV) centre and related capabilities
questions.where: House of Lords, written questions HL5015 to HL5017
questions.body: The Budget provides £70m over two years for a National Exposure and Real Time Vulnerability (NERV) centre and related capabilities. NERV will sit within the NCSC, with initial operating capability, subject to detailed planning, expected in mid-2027.
questions.why: The answer describes scaling existing NCSC capabilities to identify and notify exposed organisations, particularly in critical sectors, more quickly.
questions.linkText: Written question HL5015 (see also HL5016, HL5017)

questions.why: The question seeks a publication timetable and asks whether the plan will include workforce measures.

questions.title: AI chatbots: Meta AI and the scope of the Online Safety Act
questions.where: House of Commons, written questions 43525 and 43527
questions.why: The answers distinguish existing duties for regulated user-to-user or search services from powers to extend illegal-content duties to currently unregulated AI chatbots.

questions.title: Child-safety measures for AI chatbots
questions.body: The Government set out planned measures for AI chatbots, including preventing under-18s from accessing sexual AI chatbots or sexualised features and introducing mandatory breaks, and said regulations are being developed “at pace”.
questions.why: The answer describes planned under-18 safeguards; it does not provide a specific implementation date.

questions.title: Online Safety Act: duty to report child sexual exploitation and abuse to the NCA
questions.body: The Government confirmed that the Online Safety Act child sexual exploitation and abuse (CSEA) reporting duty has been in force since April 2026 for in-scope user-to-user services. It requires providers to report detected and unreported CSEA content to the NCA.
questions.why: This is a compliance duty for in-scope user-to-user services.

questions.title: AI to detect online drug sales
questions.where: House of Lords, written question HL5230
questions.body: The answer refers to the national PoliceAI centre and to Ofcom's fining powers in relation to online drug sales.
questions.why: This covers law enforcement use of AI and online safety enforcement.

questions.why: The answer records the Government's stated UK–EU cooperation on economic security and supply chains; today's Lords debate concerns the summit.
